sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why do GDP and per capita income not effectively measure the quality of people's life?
questions.answer: GDP ignores leisure, environmental quality, freedom, social justice and gender equality. Per capita income is only an average and does not show inequality of income, so it cannot tell whether the benefits of development reach the poor and disadvantaged.

questions.q: Differentiate between diversity and disparity with examples.
questions.answer: Diversity is a natural difference between regions — e.g. the fertile Ganga plain versus hilly, forested North-East. Disparity is a human-made inequality in income, industry, literacy, health or roads — e.g. Kerala's 90.92% literacy versus Bihar's 47.53% (2001).

questions.q: Mention any two indicators of socio-economic development.
questions.answer: Any two: per capita income / GDP; literacy rate; life expectancy; level of employment; infant mortality; access to health care.

questions.q: What is sustainable development? Give one example.
questions.answer: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Example: using solar or wind energy and rainwater harvesting instead of over-using coal and groundwater.

questions.q: Why are the tribal areas of central India underdeveloped?
questions.answer: They were neglected under colonial rule because they had little commercial value, have hilly forested terrain and poor infrastructure, few industries, and low economic and human development of local people.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain any three causes of regional disparities in India.
questions.answer: (1) Historical — areas not useful to the British, like tribal Central and North-East India, were neglected. (2) Geographical — deserts of Rajasthan and hilly terrain of the North-East restrict development; remoteness from national markets. (3) Lack of infrastructure and poor governance — States without roads, power and law and order cannot attract investment or use funds well.

questions.q: Describe the three-pronged strategy adopted for the empowerment of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
questions.answer: (1) Social empowerment — education with free books, no fees, mid-day meals, scholarships, hostels, coaching, Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya. (2) Economic empowerment — loans and support from NSFDC, NSKFDC, NSTFDC, SC/ST Development Corporations and marketing help from TRIFED. (3) Social justice — protective laws such as the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955, Prevention of Atrocities Act 1989 and Forest Rights Act 2006.

questions.q: Explain any three measures taken by the government for the economic and social empowerment of women.
questions.answer: (1) Poverty eradication and training programmes addressed to women's needs, especially in agriculture. (2) Labour laws, social security and support services such as crèches to help women work in industry. (3) Equal access to education, health and nutrition and elimination of violence against women; politically, one-third reservation in local bodies.

or.q: What is the role of the National Rural Health Mission? Mention any two other health programmes for women and children.
or.answer: Medical facilities are concentrated in cities, so NRHM was launched to provide accessible, affordable health care in rural areas, reducing the rural–urban gap. Other programmes: Janani Suraksha Yojana, Balika Samridhi Yojana, Kishori Shakti Yojana (any two).

questions.q: Describe any three measures adopted to reduce drop-out rates and improve achievement in schools.
questions.answer: (1) Creating parental awareness and mobilising the community and Panchayati Raj Institutions. (2) Economic incentives — free education, free books and uniforms, scholarships. (3) Mid-day Meal Scheme and improvement in the content and process of schooling.

questions.q: What are the goals of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan?
questions.answer: (1) Enrolment of all children of 6–14 years in school or alternative centres. (2) Bridging gender and social category gaps at the primary and elementary levels. (3) Universal retention and elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis on education for life.

questions.q: How is human development different from economic development?
questions.answer: (1) Economic development focuses mainly on income and wealth; human development enlarges all choices of people — health, education, freedom, culture. (2) Human development puts people at the centre; income is only one component. (3) It cares about quality and distribution of growth, measured by HDI (life expectancy, education, standard of living) rather than GDP alone.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What is the Human Development Index? Explain its three indices and dimensions, and state India's position.
questions.answer: HDI, developed in 1990 by economists including Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, is used by UNDP in its annual Human Development Report to measure a country's level of development. (1) A long and healthy life — life expectancy at birth. (2) Knowledge and education — adult literacy rate and combined gross enrolment ratio. (3) A decent standard of living — GDP per capita at purchasing power parity in US$. India is in the medium category near the bottom — 128 of 177 countries in 2007–08 — showing that high growth has not yet improved quality of life for all.

or.q: Explain the major efforts made for 'Education for All' in India.
or.answer: (1) National Policy on Education 1986 — free and compulsory education up to 14. (2) 86th Amendment 2002 and RTE Act 2009 — education a Fundamental Right for 6–14. (3) Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 2001 — enrolment, bridging gender and social gaps, retention, quality. (4) Mid-day Meal Scheme — nutrition and attendance. (5) National Literacy Mission 1988 — adult literacy through Total Literacy Campaign, Post Literacy and Continuing Education. (6) Results — primary schools within 1 km for 95% of rural people; literacy 52.21% (1991) to 65.37% (2001); more girls, SC and ST children enrolled.

questions.q: Why are there regional imbalances and socio-economic disparities in India? Analyse any six factors.
questions.answer: (1) Colonial history — areas of no commercial interest were ignored. (2) Geography — deserts and difficult hilly terrain. (3) Unequal distribution and poor use of natural resources (Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa). (4) Remoteness from national markets (North-East). (5) Lack of basic infrastructure — roads, electricity, transport — which discourages investment. (6) Poor governance and law-and-order problems, leading to under-use of allocated funds. These show up as differences in per capita income, poverty, industry, agriculture, literacy and roads.
